newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian Socialists unveil legislative programme.
newsitem.headline: Albanian Socialists unveil legislative programme.

text.p: Albania's Socialist-led coalition unveiled a programme for the new parliament on Sunday, pledging to boost the prime minister's powers and compensate pyramid investors as much as possible.
The collapse of shady, get-rich-quick pyramid schemes early this year triggered mass rioting that mushroomed into an anti-government revolt and widespread anarchy.

Internationally-monitored elections were held on June 29 and July 6 as a pivotal step towards ending chaos in the poor, formerly communist Balkan country and fostering economic reconstruction and modernisation.

Socialist leader Fatos Nano appealed to intellectuals and Western-trained specialists to return to Albania to join his administration, guaranteeing them "a very favourable climate of cooperation, promotion, and a professional career to their own and new Albania's benefit".

With all but two seats decided, Albania's electoral commission said the Socialists had 99 seats in the 153-seat parliament, plus another 15 held by their coalition allies, giving the new government a two-thirds majority needed for major legislative changes.

President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party was slashed back to 29 seats. The Democrats were unable to campaign in the lawless south, but its decisive defeat even in the capital Tirana and former strongholds such as Kavaje put paid to any serious claims of electoral manipulation.
Run-offs in Fier, south of Tirana, and Puke in the north, were taking place on Sunday.

Once a new government is in place, its main tasks will be restoring law and order in a country with a million looted guns in private hands, and resolving the economic chaos left by the pyramid debacle.

A statement from the Socialists and two allied parties published in the daily Koha Jone said Albania would be a parliamentary republic, with executive power concentrated in the hands of the prime minister controlled by parliament, rather than in the president.
"The president will have a non-party and non-executive role as a symbol of national unity," it said.

A headline in the daily said Nano would model his executive powers on those of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, reducing the head of state's powers which grew dramatically under the authoritarian Berisha.

The statement listed as priorities restoring public order; reorganising and depoliticising the police; a new constitution; judicial reform; privatisation of large and medium-sized enterprises; further liberalisation of the economy; and the establishment of private banks.
The programme pledged "full transparency" for pyramid investments, promising "the return and compensation up to the maximum possible limits of the money lost in pyramid schemes".
Another four high-interest investment schemes are largely frozen but still paying out small sums and will be investigated by foreign auditors to determine their viability.

"The centre-left government is a clear, responsible, broad, legitimate and stable alternative capable of governing the country. It offers concrete proposals to the Albanian electorate and guarantees to the international community," the parties said.
Berisha's cabinet resigned in March and a national unity administration was appointed to prepare elections. Western diplomats are pressing for the new parliament to get to work.

Berisha, who has pledged to step aside as president once the new government is in place, is expected to take over the leadership of the Democratic Party, replacing chairman Tritan Shehu, who resigned on Monday.
Albania's new president is expected to be Socialist party Secretary-General Rexhep Mejdani, a 52-year-old physics professor.

Nano, who was jailed by Berisha on corruption charges which the Socialists said were politically motivated, has insisted his reformed party has nothing in common with the Stalinist regime of Enver Hoxha that ruled for 45 years.
Diplomats expect Nano's government to continue market reforms, cooperate with international financial institutions and reform state institutions which crumbled earlier this year.
The electoral commission promised to announce the final results of a referendum on the monarchy this week.
Preliminary results showed about one third of voters supported restoring self-proclaimed King Leka.
